h1: Mugs and steins versus thin glass and what each does to beer
title: Mugs and Steins vs Thin Glass for Beer | Craft Beer School
desc: What a heavy mug or stein does to beer compared with thin glass: temperature, aroma, head and colour, plus when each one makes sense.
teaser: A frosted mug feels cold in the hand. What it does to the beer inside is less flattering.
standfirst: Heavy mugs and steins have centuries of beer hall history behind them. Thin glass has the sensory arguments on its side. Which one you choose changes how cold the beer stays, how much you smell and what you see. Here is the trade off in plain terms.
sections: Thick walls change the temperature of the beer

A heavy glass mug can weigh two to three times as much as a thin pint glass. All that glass has to reach the temperature of the beer. If the mug starts at room temperature, which in much of India means 28 to 35 °C, it pulls heat into a 4 °C lager for the first few minutes and the beer warms faster than it would in thin glass.

If the mug starts cold, the same mass works the other way and keeps the beer cooler for longer. That is the case for mugs in a hot beer garden. It only holds if the bar actually stores them cold, which many do not.

There is a hygiene angle too. Heavy mugs take longer to cool after a hot glasswasher cycle, so on a busy night they often go back into service still warm. A bar that wants cold mugs needs enough stock to let each one rest in the fridge for at least an hour between uses, so plan stock for the peak hour rather than the average.
Frozen mugs cause more trouble than they solve

The frosted mug from the freezer is a common sight in Indian bars. It feels like the ultimate cold beer. In practice it causes three problems. Beer hitting a surface well below 0 °C can form ice crystals, which act as nucleation points and make the beer foam over. A film of frozen water on the glass melts into the beer and thins it. Very cold beer also tastes of very little, because aroma compounds stay locked in the liquid.

A glass stored in a cold room or fridge at 2 to 4 °C gives all the benefit without the ice. A quick cold water rinse before pouring is the simplest fix of all.
Steins come from beer hall tradition

The German stein and the one litre Mass glass of Munich beer halls are working vessels. They are tough, hold a lot of beer and survive being clinked hard. Stoneware steins, often with hinged pewter lids, have a long history in German speaking countries. The lid kept out insects and debris in outdoor drinking.

A stoneware stein is opaque. You cannot see the colour, clarity or head of the beer. That did not matter much when people knew exactly what the local brewery made. It matters more when you want to judge a beer.
Thin glass shows the beer and its head

A thin, clear glass is the best window into a beer. You can see whether a lager is bright or hazy, whether the colour matches the style and whether bubbles rise in fine streams or cling to the sides. Clinging bubbles usually mean a dirty glass. Our guide to the beer clean glass test explains why.

Thin glass also tracks the temperature of the beer closely, so the beer warms slowly and evenly in your hand. That makes it easier to notice how flavour changes as a beer moves from 4 to 8 °C.
Shape matters more than thickness for aroma

Most mugs and steins are straight sided or flare slightly. They let aroma escape freely, which is fine for a crisp lager where refreshment is the point. A thin glass that narrows at the top, like a tulip or a teku, holds aroma above the beer. That is why aromatic beers sit better in stemmed glassware.

Thickness itself does little to aroma. A thin straight tumbler releases aroma about as freely as a thick straight mug. What you gain with thin glass is clarity, lightness and a closer feel of the beer's temperature.
The handle has a real job

The one clear advantage of a mug is the handle. It keeps a warm hand off the glass, so the beer warms more slowly than in a pint glass held in the palm. On a 1 litre serving that you will drink over 40 minutes, that matters.

It also makes a big, heavy glass easier to hold, especially when it is wet. For a session lager in a beer garden on a warm evening, a cold mug with a handle is a sensible choice. Just make sure it is cold from the fridge, not the freezer.

• Cold mug or stein: session lagers, Munich helles and Märzen, outdoor drinking, big servings, a festival atmosphere.
  • Thin straight glass: lagers, pale ales and stouts where you want to see the beer and drink at a steady pace.
  • Thin stemmed glass: aromatic or strong beers where smell matters more than volume.

None of these is wrong. The mistake is serving a delicate hoppy beer in a frozen mug, then wondering why it tastes of nothing. Brewers check every batch in clean, thin glass for a reason: it hides nothing. Our guide to true to brand tasting shows how they do it.
Run a quick side by side

Your first step: take two cans of the same lager from the fridge. Pour one into a room temperature mug and one into a thin glass rinsed with cold water. Taste both after five minutes and again after fifteen. Note which one stays cold and which one smells of more. You will have your own answer in under half an hour.
faqs: Is a frozen mug good for beer?
Not really. Ice crystals make the beer foam, melted frost waters it down and very cold beer hides its aroma. A fridge cold glass is better.
Does a thick mug keep beer colder?
Only if it starts cold. A room temperature mug warms the beer faster than thin glass because it holds more heat.
Why do German beer halls use steins?
They are tough, hold a large serving and survive being clinked. Stoneware steins with lids also kept insects out in outdoor drinking.
